title: Non-QM Loans: Helping Buyers Who Don't Fit the Standard Box
description: Self-employed buyers, investors, and borrowers with recent credit events often need non-QM loans. An agent's guide to the options and when to use them.
image_alt: A person in an orange shirt writing on white paper

faq.a: Non-QM stands for non-qualified mortgage: a loan that doesn't meet the federal Qualified Mortgage definition or agency guidelines, but still requires the lender to verify the borrower's ability to repay.
Not inherently. They use different documentation or guidelines and usually cost more, but lenders must still verify ability to repay.

faq.q: How long do non-QM loans take to close?
faq.a: Often similar to other loans when documents are ready. Getting the file reviewed early is the best way to avoid surprises.

body_html:
Every agent eventually meets a buyer who's clearly successful and clearly ready to buy, yet keeps hearing "no" from traditional lenders. Maybe they own a business, have complex investment income, or had a credit event a couple of years ago. Non-QM financing exists for exactly these buyers, and knowing the basics helps you keep deals alive.

What non-QM means

A Qualified Mortgage, or QM, is a loan that meets federal standards and typically agency guidelines from Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, FHA, or VA. A non-QM loan falls outside those standards, usually because of how income is documented or because of the borrower's profile. Lenders still must make a good-faith determination that the borrower can repay. They simply use different evidence.

Common non-QM programs

ProgramWho it helps
Bank statement loansSelf-employed borrowers whose tax returns understate cash flow
DSCR loansInvestors qualifying on rental income instead of personal income
Asset-based or asset depletionBorrowers with substantial assets but irregular income
1099-onlyIndependent contractors with consistent 1099 earnings
Recent credit event programsBorrowers a short time past a bankruptcy, foreclosure, or short sale
Non-warrantable condo financingBuyers of units in projects that don't meet agency standards

I go deeper on two of the most common in my posts on bank statement loans and DSCR loans.

What to tell your buyers up front

  • Pricing is usually higher than conventional financing, reflecting the different risk profile.
  • Down payment expectations are often larger.
  • Some loans have prepayment penalties, especially investor products.
  • Many buyers refinance later into conventional loans once their documentation fits standard guidelines.

How agents can spot a non-QM buyer early

  1. The buyer is self-employed and mentions big write-offs
  2. The buyer has been turned down by a bank despite strong income or assets
  3. The buyer is purchasing an investment property inside an LLC
  4. The buyer had a bankruptcy, foreclosure, or short sale in recent years
  5. The property is a condo with a high investor concentration or litigation

Getting these buyers to a loan officer early, before they fall in love with a house, is the single most helpful thing you can do.

Why a broker matters here

Non-QM guidelines vary dramatically from one lender to the next. One may allow 12 months of bank statements while another requires 24. One may accept a recent credit event while another won't. As a broker, my team can shop multiple non-QM lenders for the best fit, which often makes the difference between a closed deal and a lost one.

A note on timing and documentation

Non-QM files often move just as quickly as traditional loans, but they rely more on getting documentation right the first time. Bank statements need to be complete, business ownership needs to be verified, and large deposits need explanations. When agents encourage buyers to gather these documents before writing offers, closings stay on track.

  • Bank statement borrowers: 12 or 24 months of complete statements, plus proof of business ownership
  • Investors: leases or rent estimates, entity documents if using an LLC, and insurance quotes
  • Recent credit events: dates and documentation of the event, such as discharge papers

Explaining non-QM to sellers

Some listing agents hesitate when they hear "non-QM." A short, confident explanation helps: the buyer has been fully reviewed under a program designed for their situation, the lender is verifying ability to repay, and the loan officer is available to answer questions. When your buyer's financing is presented clearly, a non-QM offer can be just as strong as any other.

The takeaway

A "no" from a bank isn't always the final word. Non-QM programs open the door for self-employed buyers, investors, and borrowers rebuilding credit. Know the main programs, set expectations about pricing, and connect these buyers with a loan officer early. You'll keep deals that would otherwise disappear.
